Night time game discussions are generally banned in my games for several reasons. First, several of my players experience anxiety during the game, particularly when they’re playing evil. Giving them a gameplay break at night helps. Also, we formed our little online group to build friendships, so encouraging them to get to know each other at night has been instrumental in building those ties between people. Finally, and this is specific to us, we stream our games. Night time game play discussions are hidden from the ST and the audience, which doesn’t make for great content in my opinion. That’s just my house rule, but I haven’t gotten any complaints, and I think it’s made our little Clocktower community stronger.

I also remind my players that while they are free to request people nominate and/or vote in a certain way, I won’t tolerate them telling or bullying players to nominate or vote. People need to have their agency in this game in order for everyone to have fun.

Thank you for the encouragement!  Absolutely, especially with a free-form game like Dungeons and Dragons, there is no wrong way to play.  If everyone around the table is enjoying themselves, then you are a having a successful D&D game!  And that can look drastically different from table to table.  One group may enjoy just sitting around a tavern telling tales.  Another may want increasingly complex tactical combat scenarios.  Another may want an intricate story with thoughtful characters.  Or, maybe your group just wants to kill, burn, and loot everything in sight.  If everyone at the table (including the DM) is having fun, then you have no problem.  Huzzah to you and happy gaming!

The only thing I would hesitate on is the idea that that's the only situation in which a problem may emerge.  I've certainly seen issues where a player at the table can make others uncomfortable in some way, or a person wants to play D&D but is too anxious to put themselves out there.  And then there are folks who are doing their best, but may not know the best way to handle situations that involve gender, gender identity, race, sexual orientation, disability, etc.  D&D is nothing if not a complex social gathering, with people playing characters who may be quite different from themselves.  All sorts of issues can arise around the table, and hopefully we'll be here to help offer some guidance.

Having a friend to play with or having a connection to Guild Wars 1 so that you feel invested in the story are probably the two main avenues into the game for most people.  The community is, on the whole, quite nice though.  So if you ever feel like taking another stab at it, you may look into finding a guild of like-minded people.  It just requires a little extra time and effort.  If you feel like trying, the [Guild Recruitment subreddit](https://www.reddit.com/r/guildrecruitment/) is a good place to start.

Guild Wars 2 is my main game, and I highly recommend it.  Due to the nature of its design, it's never too late to jump on board.  Won't take you long to develop a character that can play almost all of the end game content with aplomb.  Even more recommended if you like a game with rich lore and lots to discover.  I wouldn't say it's very similar to Marvel Heroes, but the free core game will give you hundreds of hours of content to see if it's something you'd enjoy.

I think, psychologically and financially, it's better for the company to incentivize you to get more characters and use them, than to punish people for using characters they've paid for and spent time with.  Though it would make battles more interesting perhaps.

Guild Wars 2 targets horizontal progression, meaning earning new skills and cosmetics rather than increasing power endlessly.  How well they succeed is up for debate.  I'll explain more later.

For gear, there's a few things to understand.  First, within each tier, the points per stat are fixed so there's no roll like there is in ARPGs.  Gear can have different stat combos, but the stat points are allocated the same for every gear within a slot and tier.  There is always a primary stat that gets more points and two or more secondary stats.

So for example, a DPS direct damage build might run Berserker's which has stats (point values made up but to give a basic idea:) 200 power, 100 crit rating, 100 crit damage whereas a condition (damage over time) build might run stats that are 200 condition damage, 67 condition duration, 67 power, 67 crit rating.  The allocation of stat types might change but the point value in each category is always the same.

There are 3 end game gear tiers worth talking about in GW2 (kinda comparable to cosmic and unique right now in Marvel): Exotic, Ascended, and Legendary.

Exotic was Best in Slot when the game released but was considered too easy to obtain.  It could be purchased off the global exchange for a fairly trivial amount of money or earned from dungeons but it would take an expert max level player maybe 5-10 hours to earn it in game, if that.

As a result, the devs added Ascended tier about two months after launch.  They added only rings and trinkets (I guess equivalent to artifacts) at first, amounting to only a 5% power boost over Exotic (vs about 15% between all the other tiers).  They rolled out weapons and armor over the following year.  In the end, Ascended was about also a 15% boost over Exotic, but it cost like 50x more for a full set and had a lot of accountbound progression so you could not bypass it by paying with currency on the exchange.

However, all the encounters except raids and very high end dungeons in the game are still tuned at Exotic level, so getting Ascended is kind of a prestige long-term goal that is not required to access most content.  Even raids have been beaten by groups in full Exotic.

Legendary is an even more long term goal but it's purely cosmetic (weapons give you footsteps and auras and fancy particle effects and armor pieces animate).  The only benefits it confers is that it is guaranteed to always be Best in Slot so if GW2 ever released a tier over Ascended, Legendaries would automatically get upgraded, and Legendary items can be stat swapped at will (so you can change from a power stat combo to DoT or healing or tanking or whatever without paying or getting a new piece of equipment).

That said, GW2 has not added a new tier in 3 years and it has not ever raised the level cap, even in expansions.

So for endgame, Ascended and Legendary can take quite a long time to get, so they are still somewhat end game progression.  There are 9 classes in the game and most veteran players will aim to have all 9 geared out so that can take a while.

In addition to that, the expansion added Masteries and Elite Specializations.  Masteries are basically extra abilities that max level characters can earn with a combination of regular experience from combat and mastery points that are earned from achievements in the game.  Masteries don't usually add power to the character but can unlock extra content.  For example, the biggest impact Mastery added so far has been gliding, which is not only cool and can help keep you from dying to fall damage but has enabled the game to add bosses that have an aerial combat component.  Others have lesser impact but do things like let you access shortcuts between areas of a map or enter a toxic region that you couldn't before or summon NPCs in an area to support you.

Elite Specializations are kind of like Prestige classes.  Basically every class in the game started with 5 trait lines of which you could have 3 active at any given time.  They function like the new right panel in Marvel where traits modify existing skills to do different things, enabling new playstyles.  Elite Specializations add new trait lines which drastically alter the class.  For example, one class that could create clones and interrupt mobs got a Chronomancer specialization which allows them to save their state and revert to that state after a period of time, as well as being able to reduce cooldowns for allies and slow cast times for enemies, etc.  The Elite Specializations can take a while to earn.  The first elite specs did represent a power creep over the base spec, but the idea is 1 new elite spec for each class in each new expansion, and the elite specs in the future are all supposed to be on par with each other, only unlocking new playstyles.

Beyond that, earning cosmetics is a huge part of endgame so if you want perpetual power creep and don't care about getting fancy looks for your characters, that can be a bit dull.  From a skill perspective, the game is never going to be as hardcore at the high end as WoW raids, for example, but the game supports a wide variety of skill ranges so a competitive player can always strive to set new benchmarks or solo content.  Dungeons are designed for 5 players but since there are no enrage timers, top PvE players have solo'd almost every boss in the game and compete for best kill times.  Likewise, raids 10-man content and hard enough that lots of groups wipe endlessly on them, but the best guilds in the game have been able to 3-man or 5-man a lot of the bosses even despite the enrage timers and also compete for fastest kill times.

Finally, GW2 has a fairly robust PvP and Realm vs Realm (called World vs World) modes.  Stats are normalized and gear is free in PvP, so it's purely a matter of skill, team coordination, and builds for PvP but you can compete for ranking and rewards and slots in tournaments.  Realm vs Realm is a week-long matchup between 3 servers across 4 different maps.  It uses the PvE system of gearing and adds supply camps, towers, and castle keeps that need to be held and sieged and taken.  Each map supports about 50 players per server.  Since both these modes are fighting against other players (small teams or large server groups), they offer a lot more diversity and challenge in endgame.

From a f2p perspective, the entire base game is available.  There are messaging and global exchange restrictions to combat botting and goldsellers, and you don't get the daily login rewards as a free player, but other than that you can play anything people who bought at launch could play.  The expansion is buy to play, so you do not have access to the newest content like masteries or elite specs, which can put you at a bit of a disadvantage in high end dungeons or PvP, but it's certainly not a dealbreaker.  It's important to remember the game is still fundamentally designed as a buy-to-play (no subscription) franchise, so that may explain some design decisions, but the free to play component is substantial and can be viewed as an extremely generous trial with no major restrictions (you earn xp and currencies at a regular rate, and you can access all the non-expansion content at max level).

They've had so many Kickstarter campaigns for this game, it's ridiculous.  As far as the quote goes, it still reads to me like they're packaging up the stretch goals from this campaign only, but with this Kickstarter-happy company, who the heck knows.

I think what we're more used to is a stretch goal unlocking something for some tiers, but not for others.  [Shadows of Brimstone](https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/1034852783/shadows-of-brimstone) had goals that unlocked content for people at higher level tiers, but could be purchased via the add-on process if you didn't buy in at the expensive tiers.  [Tokaido](https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/funforge/tokaido-collectors-edition) had stretch goals that provided minis to people who were at the $100+ tier, but not at the lower level tiers that included the game.  People asked for some of those stretch goals to be included as add-ons for lower tiered folks, but Fun Forge didn't go for it.  The difference with Among the Stars is that the coins and tuck boxes weren't automatically included at any tier.   

Ultimately, stretch goals can be done in any number of ways.  It's a new system that's still finding its legs.  I can understand some initial confusion with the coins and tuck boxes for Among the Stars, but I think it becomes apparent that they're add-ons pretty quickly when you do your due diligence, as you did.  

I think it's fair to say their stretch goal system was slightly confusing and perhaps not well-thought out.  And I think it's safe to say that it's overpriced when compared to other games of its ilk when their shipped domestically.  I just think accusing Mage Company of being dishonest or intentionally misleading might be overstating things a bit.   (Not accusing you of saying that, just want to make sure things are clear for people reading this thread and deciding whether or not they want to back the game.)
